title: Under the Cherry Blossom
summary: An interactive VR experience that lets users stir, lift, and scatter falling cherry blossom petals through natural mid-air hand gestures.

paragraph: Under the Cherry Blossom is an interactive VR artwork that lets users stir, lift, and scatter falling petals with their bare hands.
Combining hand tracking with simulated fluid flow, it turns a fleeting encounter with cherry blossoms into an immersive experience that blends familiar motion with playful possibilities.
Cherry blossom petals scattering in the wind create a beautiful but fleeting spectacle.
Their brief season and sensitivity to weather make this moment difficult to experience in person.
Inspired by this transience and its presence in art, the project explores how VR can recreate the scene and extend the ways people interact with it.
A formative study used small pieces of tissue paper as artificial petals to explore how people wanted to interact with them.
Participants tried catching, sweeping, and throwing the petals, as well as arranging them into patterns.
They also wanted their hands to generate stronger currents than air normally allows, more like moving through water.
These observations guided the focus on stirring, lifting, and scattering petals through hand gestures.
The system combines a 3D fluid simulation, petal-like particles, and mid-air gesture interaction.
Extending Jos Stam's 'Real-Time Fluid Dynamics for Games' into three dimensions, it uses a simplified, liquid-like flow to create responsive, visually convincing motion.
Petals move and rotate in response to the surrounding flow and their orientation, producing varied, fluttering movements.
Oculus hand tracking translates hand movement and openness into fluid flow: an open palm creates a stronger current than a closed fist.
The current is directed mainly by the palm's orientation, allowing users to guide petals intuitively by sweeping their hands through the scene.
The prototype demonstrated relatively natural interaction between hands, fluid flow, and virtual petals.
Future work could explore direct contact with petals, interaction with those gathered on the ground, and shared experiences, while refining the simulation and the artwork.
The course project from [Interactive Universe Design - Spring 2022, instructor: Prof. Seokhyung Bae]
